sources.source: Google — Site Reliability Engineering, Chapter 22, Addressing Cascading Failures

items.item: A cascading failure is a failure that grows over time as a result of positive feedback, occurring when one portion of a system failing increases the probability other portions fail.

at.step: Hook: the dashboard says fine, the partition says otherwise

items.item: The most common cause of cascading failures is overload.

at.step: Reveal: a failure, named, radius, detection, recovery, loss, time

items.item: Queued requests consume memory and increase latency.

at.step: Reveal: a failure, named, radius, detection, recovery, loss, time

items.item: Always use randomized exponential backoff when scheduling retries.

at.step: Predict: what actually ends the crash loop?

sources.source: Marc Brooker — Exponential Backoff and Jitter (AWS Architecture Blog, 2015)

items.item: N clients compete in the first round, N-1 in the second round, and so on, under contention.

at.step: Predict: what actually ends the crash loop?

items.item: Capped exponential backoff means clients multiply their backoff by a constant after each attempt, up to some maximum value.

at.step: Predict: what actually ends the crash loop?

items.item: A failure table's six columns (failure, blast radius, detection, recovery, data lost, time to recover) turn a vague worry into something checkable, one row at a time.

at.step: Reveal: a failure, named, radius, detection, recovery, loss, time

items.item: Blast radius is scoped to what shares a failure domain, not to what shares a dashboard — an averaged metric can bury a real, narrower failure.

at.step: Reveal: blast radius is a failure domain, not a dashboard

items.item: An empty recovery cell is itself the finding, not a detail to fill in on faith.

at.step: Reveal: an empty recovery cell is the finding

items.item: RPO and RTO are two different numbers, each priced separately — tightening one doesn't tighten the other for free.

at.step: Reveal: RPO and RTO are two different numbers

items.item: RPO and RTO are set per data class, not once for a whole system — a system-wide target overpays for data that can tolerate loss.

at.step: Reveal: RPO and RTO are set per data class

items.item: A degraded mode is a designed trade that names, up front, exactly what it gives up — not an accident of what happened to keep working.

at.step: Reveal: two degraded modes, two different trades

items.item: The failure table's five columns don't depend on what kind of failure it is — applying them to a new failure finds whatever gap exists the same way.

at.step: Prove it: a different failure, the same table

items.item: This topic leaves out disaster-recovery mechanics, game days, incident response, and the replication/consensus mechanics that set an achievable RPO deliberately — it teaches the design response, not the mechanics.
Failure-mode enumeration via a failure table and RPO/RTO budgeting per data class are established practice, not an emerging technique.

This topic gives the shop a failure table, a priced RPO/RTO budget per data class, and two degraded modes, which the next topic (cost model and dominant cost lever) assumes already exist before pricing the whole design.
